The current coalition in Johannesburg includes the ANC, EFF, PA, AIC, IFP and Al Jama-ah. Mama says the party will not work with the DA because of its stance on Israel and Palestine. “We will speak to all parties except one. Al Jama-ah is diametrically opposed to Zionists. Period. We stand with the people of Palestine. We don’t receive any Israeli funds. So the only party we won’t work with is the DA. But if so all other parties we were we we’re open to completely.” Al Jama-ah’s 2026 Manifesto Launch is here! Watch here: https://t.co/sSGJTW6KgU #AlJamaAh #LGE2026 https://t.co/fe4gRBWoVY — Al Jama-ah (@Aljama_ah) October 17, 2026 Meanwhile, the party has pledged to address water and sanitation challenges if elected in the upcoming local government elections. Its plans include upgrading bulk sewer infrastructure, clearing blocked pipelines and introducing strict five-year preventative maintenance schedules. The party launched its 12-point election manifesto in Orlando, Soweto, this Saturday afternoon. It has also promised to deploy ward-based rapid repair teams to fix water leaks, reduce water losses through smart meters and upgrade neglected township and suburban roads. Al Jama-ah President Ganief Hendricks says many communities still lack access to basic services. “Like I said earlier on at the Hector Peterson Museum, our mothers must still take the buckets to the river and fetch the water. items.summary: Eskom has warned against placing election posters on electricity infrastructure, due to safety risks. It says posters on electricity poles, transformers and substations can damage critical infrastructure. The power utility appealed to people not to place election posters, banners, or any promotional material on electricity infrastructure. The warning comes less than three weeks ahead of the Local Government Elections set for the 4th of November. items.originalTitle: 'Cockroach' party founder released from Indian police custody
items.author: Siya Tsewu
items.title: 'Cockroach' party founder released from Indian police custody
items.summary: 'Cockroach' party founder released from Indian police custody Siya Tsewu Sat, 10/17/2026 - 14:36 NEW DELHI - India's Cockroach Janata Party founder Abhijeet Dipke was released from detention on Saturday, a day after his arrest during a police crackdown on protests against the election authority. Dipke, 31, was detained on Friday in New Delhi as he headed to join a rally that the CJP protest movement had called in the capital's central Connaught Place district. He walked out of a police station on Saturday afternoon, waving to the media and giving a thumbs up as he was driven away, an AFP photographer saw. "Abhijeet Dipke released," CJP legal affairs chief Ratna Singh said on social media. Opposition parties and CJP activists have defied a security crackdown, rallying to demand the resignation of India's chief election commissioner after accusing the poll body of manipulating voter rolls to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling party. The commission, which oversees voting in the world's most populous nation, has denied any wrongdoing. Two other senior CJP leaders, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, were arrested on October 14 after entering Jantar Mantar, a decades-old protest site that police have declared off-limits for demonstrations. They remain in custody. Members of Modi's Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party have long alleged that large numbers of undocumented Muslim migrants from neighbouring Bangladesh have fraudulently entered India's electoral rolls. Rights groups and critics however say Modi's government has eroded democratic freedoms during more than a decade in power, citing pressure on journalists, civil society groups and political opponents -- allegations the government rejects. Article by AFP

items.originalTitle: Clashes hit French cities over cost of living
items.author: Preggie Moodley
items.title: Clashes hit French cities over cost of living
items.summary: French police charged on protesters in Paris on Saturday (October 17) as some of the most violent protests in years over living costs and public services drew thousands onto the streets. The protests began last month at high schools in Paris’ poor northern suburbs , where anger over teacher shortages and shabby facilities evolved into a broader movement focused on inequality, public spending and living standards. French President Emmanuel Macron, who urged calm on Friday, is entering the final stretch of his presidency amid a fragmented political landscape and growing pressure over the economy. France’s efforts to reduce public debt have failed to reassure investors, pushing government borrowing costs to their highest levels in more than two decades.

items.originalTitle: Nepal floods 'defining moment' for climate action: UN
items.author: Siya Tsewu
items.title: Nepal floods 'defining moment' for climate action: UN
items.summary: Nepal floods 'defining moment' for climate action: UN Siya Tsewu Sat, 10/17/2026 - 14:17 KATHMANDU - Nepal's devastating floods should be a turning point for global climate action, with the international community helping the Himalayan nation recover, a top UN official told AFP on Saturday. The country suffered one of the worst disasters in its history on August 26, when a mountain collapse near the China border triggered catastrophic floods that killed more than 1,400 people and left over 5,000 missing. Scientists said climate change played a significant role in that disaster. Jorge Moreira da Silva, executive director of the UN Office for Project Services (UNOPS), which implements humanitarian and development projects, said he had witnessed "massive devastation" during a visit to affected communities. Nepal, a largely rural country of 30 million people that contributes little to global greenhouse gas emissions, estimates reconstruction will cost $4.78 billion. "This is a defining moment not only for Nepal, this is a defining moment for the international community," Moreira da Silva told AFP in Kathmandu. "It's not fair to ask a country that emits almost nothing of CO2 to suddenly pay alone the consequence of something that was not generated by the country," he added. "That's why it's fundamental that global solidarity is brought to this equation." - 'Climate justice' - Moreira da Silva said reconstruction and resettlement must account for future climate risks, while the international community must "renew its commitment to climate". "It's also about climate justice and climate responsibility," he said, warning that low-emitting countries would continue to bear the brunt of climate change. "This is going to happen unless those countries that emit the most... change their pathway," he said. Moreira da Silva said Nepal was rebuilding as global disruptions threatened food security. He also leads the UN task force for the Strait of Hormuz. "The simultaneous disruption of the three maritime shock points... the Strait of Hormuz, in the Black Sea and in the Red Sea, poses a significant challenge, particularly on food security," he said. The UN and its humanitarian partners launched a $49.6 million appeal last month to provide emergency assistance to flood victims. Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah told the United Nations last month that the flooding "was a warning to the world" about the growing dangers of climate change. By Paavan Mathema Article by AFP

items.originalTitle: Albanian capital sees fifth straight day of violent clashes
items.author: Siya Tsewu
items.title: Albanian capital sees fifth straight day of violent clashes
items.summary: Albanian capital sees fifth straight day of violent clashes Siya Tsewu Sat, 10/17/2026 - 14:14 TIRANA - Albania's capital Tirana saw clashes for a fifth straight day Saturday as protesters demanded the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama, who pledged to listen to their criticism. Several hundred people, some masked, gathered around noon in front of the ministry of education, with protests later spreading across the city. Protesters threw rocks at the police and set litter bins on fire, using them as barricades to prevent the police from advancing. After police officers had used megaphones to call on those gathered to desist from violence, they used water cannons and tear gas to temporarily disperse the crowd. Violent demonstrations have rocked Tirana since Tuesday, with thousands of protesters calling for Rama to step down over university conditions and high tuition fees. At the beginning of the protest demonstrators set a suitcase on fire and threw it in the education ministry courtyard, symbolically showing they do not want to leave Albania. Journalism student Sinan Billa said the protest was "a reaction to express discontent at the silence of our government." "Young people have awoken for our parents, too," Billa told AFP. "We are not asking for privileges. We are demanding our rights, our future and a better country," he said. While visiting local business damaged in the demonstrations, Rama said he respected the students and added that "their right to protest must and will be protected. "Their voices, the voices of young people and of every citizen who has taken part in protests today, must and will be heard with respect," Rama said. However, he added that he "will not allow anyone to jeopardise the future of this country". Local media reported further protests in the coastal town of Durres, where demonstrators smashed the windows of the post office and blocked roads with burning barricades. On Friday night police deployed tear gas and water cannons as protesters hurled stones at security forces, burning dustbins to block roads across the city. The clashes continued into the night in several parts of the city. Police said 10 people were arrested after Friday's demonstrations, with criminal proceedings lodged against a further 22. The health ministry said 25 people, including nine police officers, sustained minor injuries during clashes in Tirana, Vlora and Lezha on Friday. This week's escalation of unrest comes after months of anti-government protests in the Balkan nation, initially sparked by a controversial resort development linked to US President Donald Trump's family. Article by AFP

items.originalTitle: All Blacks thump Wallabies in Sydney on back of brilliant first half
items.author: Wendy Mothata
items.title: All Blacks thump Wallabies in Sydney on back of brilliant first half
items.summary: The All Blacks rode ​a first-half try blitz to a 43-21 victory over the Wallabies at Stadium Australia on Saturday, extending their ‌win streak over their trans-Tasman-Sea rivals to 13 matches. With the Bledisloe Cup already safely in the cupboard for a 24th year after last week’s 50-19 win in Auckland, New Zealand exploded out of the blocks and crushed all thoughts of an upset with six tries before the break. Despite losing Jordie ​Barrett to a calf injury before kickoff and another centre in Quinn Tupaea early on with a concussion, the All ​Blacks overwhelmed the Wallabies with power, pace and precision in the opening 40 minutes. “I’m really proud of ⁠the boys, the way we came out on that in that first half,” said New Zealand captain Codie Taylor. “It was a ​real challenge for us this week to make sure that we backed up a really good performance from last week, and I ​thought we were awesome in that first 40.” Australia showed some flashes of backline brilliance, particularly in the second half, but struggled to get hold of the ball for prolonged periods and were unable to match the accuracy or clinical finishing of the All Blacks. In a whirlwind of offloads, winger Josh ​Moorby, fullback Beauden Barrett, flanker Peter Lakai and replacement back Rieko Ioane all crossed in the first 26 minutes to give the ​visitors a quick-fire 22-0 lead. Wallabies flyhalf Declan Meredith did well to get a pass away in the tackle just before the half-hour mark to ‌send Jeremy ⁠Williams over for a try but the lock was sin-binned at the other end of the field two minutes later. All Blacks number eight Wallace Sititi immediately made the extra man count with his team’s fifth try and Beauden Barrett added a sixth, his second, off an intercept to send New Zealand into the break with a 36-7 lead. Moorby faked out the defence for his second five-pointer ​within three minutes of the restart ​before the Wallabies finally finished ⁠off a backline move for fullback Tom Wright to go over. Australia were looking stronger with their replacements on the pitch, and Meredith almost scored a try after a scything break up the ​middle, then saved a try at the other end. A clever line dropout from Wright did result ​in a third ⁠Australia try in the 66th minute for replacement back Filipo Daugunu that delighted the majority of the crowd of 73,399. New Zealand were reduced to 14 men after Samisoni Taukei’aho went off injured, and went down to 13 when debutant Chay Fihaki was shown a yellow card ⁠but managed ​to hold out the Wallabies for the last few minutes. “I’m gutted,” said Wallabies ​captain Harry Wilson. “When you give a team like the All Blacks a head start it’s tough, and it’s not good enough for this group. “We’ve got to be a ​lot better. It’s been a very disappointing series, and we’re going to have to regroup.”

items.summary: Jayawardene quits as coach of five-time IPL winners Mumbai Siya Tsewu Sat, 10/17/2026 - 14:08 MUMBAI - Mahela Jayawardene stepped down as head coach of Mumbai Indians on Saturday to end a nearly decade-long association with one of the Indian Premier League's most successful teams. The 49-year-old former Sri Lanka captain led Mumbai to three titles in his first stint between 2017 and 2022. He rejoined the team in 2024 but was unable to replicate his success as five-time IPL winners Mumbai finished fourth in 2025 and ninth out of 10 teams in 2026. "Together we have shared some unforgettable moments, overcome challenges and built something we can all be proud of," Jayawardene said in a statement. "I leave with immense pride in what we have achieved together and will always carry a special place in my heart for MI. "I wish the team every success in the years ahead." Jayawardene represented Sri Lanka in 149 Tests, 448 one-day internationals and 55 T20 matches between 1997 and 2015. Article by AFP

items.title: Egypt’s Sisi says his presidency will end in 2030
items.summary: Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Saturday that his ​presidential term would end in 2030 and ‌that the question of his departure from office was settled, reaffirming that Egypt’s constitution would ​not be amended. “I said that the ​Egyptian constitution would not be touched.” “This is an entirely settled matter ​and will not be discussed,” he added, referring ​to the end of his current term. Sisi, 71, is serving a six-year term after winning re-election ​in December 2023. Constitutional amendments approved in ​a 2019 referendum extended presidential terms to six years ‌from ⁠four and allowed Sisi to seek a third term, clearing the way for him to remain in office until 2030. A ​former general, Sisi ​rose ⁠to power in 2013 by toppling Egypt’s first democratically elected president, ​Mohamed Mursi, after mass protests against ​his ⁠rule. He made the remarks on Saturday while attending a graduation ceremony for new classes ⁠at ​the Egyptian Military Academy.

items.originalTitle: Leaders weigh 'huge benefit', risks of AI for global economy
items.author: Siya Tsewu
items.title: Leaders weigh 'huge benefit', risks of AI for global economy
items.summary: Leaders weigh 'huge benefit', risks of AI for global economy Siya Tsewu Sat, 10/17/2026 - 13:52 BANGKOK - The artificial intelligence boom has been a key driver of global growth, but also poses economic risks should investment in the technology falter, experts and policymakers said this week at the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok. Propelled by spending on data centres and microchips, AI has helped cushion the economic shock of rising global energy prices caused by war in the Middle East, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said in a report on Tuesday. The fund's chief economist Silvana Tenreyro noted this week that global trade rose 8.3 percent between 2023 and 2025, a figure she said would be closer to 4.6 percent without AI-related products. "It is everywhere in the global economy," Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem said of AI on Friday. "You see it in GDP. You see it in the stock market. You see it in the bond market... So it is here, and it's just the beginning." But some top officials gathered in Bangkok this week cautioned against relying too heavily on AI investment. Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh called AI the "most consequential change" to the global economy in his lifetime, and said it had "a huge benefit". Still, he warned the road ahead would be "bumpy". "The path from where we are to there is likely to be a very bumpy one, bumpy in our understanding of the technology, bumpy because we really don't know what the market structure is going to be of these new technologies," he said. IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva similarly noted the AI boom's boost to global growth, but she told AFP that any slowdown in the industry "would be felt across the world". "If there is loss of confidence and money runs away from AI, that can lead to financial stability risks," Georgieva said. An IMF report released this week projected that a decline in AI investment could reduce global GDP by 0.4 percent by 2028. "Weaker or less durable AI investments and profitability could be a shock that triggers a market correction," the report said. - War and regulation - While AI investment and trade have softened the global economic impact of the Middle East war, economists at Moody's Analytics have warned that if the conflict drags on it could "puncture" the boom. They said higher energy prices and tighter financial conditions could push up operating costs and interest rates, adding to doubts over "the long-term profitability and viability of AI business models". "A drawn-out conflict would put serious strain on the economics behind AI investment," the group said. The uncertainty around regulation has also clouded the technology's outlook. Leaders like US President Donald Trump have urged more limited government regulation, even as some in the industry have called for legislation to mitigate risks. Georgieva, the IMF chief, appeared on Friday to link such regulation to future investment. "If there are no safeguards, then the risks may exceed the opportunities," she said in Bangkok. By Asad Hashim Article by AFP

items.originalTitle: Kenya reports third Ebola case
items.author: Tshepiso Moche
items.title: Kenya reports third Ebola case
items.summary: Kenya reported its third Ebola infection on Friday, in a woman it said was closely related ​to the first two patients. The 65-year-old had been in quarantine since October 6, ‌the health ministry said in a statement. “Once she developed fever, sore throat and malaise, she was isolated and specimen collected for testing,” it added. “She was diagnosed early and is currently receiving supportive care improving her ​chances of recovery.” Authorities say Kenya’s cases are linked to the Ebola epidemic in Congo — the second-largest outbreak ​ever recorded, with more than 9,000 cases and more than 4,000 deaths. Kenya’s first recorded ⁠case was a man who had been ill in Congo for about a month, ​then travelled by road to Uganda and flew to Nairobi on October 3. That Kenyan man ​was driven to hospital by a relative and died on October 5. The health ministry said the second patient was in a stable condition and there was still no evidence the disease was spreading in ​the wider community. FEARS OF SCREENING LAPSES Ebola’s spread to Kenya has raised concerns about lapses ​in screening systems. The first patient managed to cross the border between Congo and Uganda, which has ‌been ⁠closed since May, and then pass through Nairobi’s busy Jomo Kenyatta International Airport. Kenyan authorities say they have contacted 127 out of the 130 people known to have come into contact with the first patient. They had all been placed into quarantine and efforts were ​under way to trace ​the remaining three. Ebola spreads ⁠through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected people, whether living or dead. The disease can cause fever, vomiting, diarrhoea and, ​in severe cases, internal and external bleeding. The outbreak in Congo was ​declared in ⁠mid-May but may have started months earlier. It is caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain, for which there are currently no approved vaccines or treatments. Uganda reported Ebola cases in May ⁠and June ​but was declared free of the virus in ​August. A doctor who returned to France in June from Congo tested positive but there have been no further ​cases there.

items.originalTitle: Trump waives key Russia-related sanctions
items.author: Tshepiso Moche
items.title: Trump waives key Russia-related sanctions
items.summary: President Donald Trump waived key Russia-related US sanctions and tariffs days before they were to take effect under a law he signed last month, including duties on the country’s goods and penalties for buying its oil and gas. In an executive order released by the White House on Friday, Trump said the ​waiver was in the national interests of the United States. The law is meant to increase pressure on Russia for its invasion ​of Ukraine that began in 2022. Trump, however, has been warming toward Russia and publicly criticizing Ukrainian ⁠President Volodymyr Zelenskiyy, including suggesting Kyiv needs a new leader. Weeks before the US midterm elections in which Trump’s Republicans are battling to ​maintain their narrow grip on both chambers of Congress, the new measures could have risked raising oil prices even further while Americans already face ​increased costs largely attributed to the US-Israeli war on Iran , analysts have said. The legislation, whose primary backer in Congress was the late Senator Lindsey Graham, a South Carolina Republican, would have imposed tariffs of up to 100% within 30 days on all goods brought into the US from the five largest importers of ​Russian crude oil or gas, as well as any country that knowingly bought oil or gas 30 days after the law was ​enacted or was among the top five countries helping Russia evade sanctions. The order said the waiver will remain in effect until Trump or his top ‌officials ⁠determine that “further action is appropriate.” Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 in mid-September. “I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States,” Trump said in the order. Countries such as China and India, which are among the biggest buyers of Russian oil, have raised concerns about the ​Russia sanctions bill. Beijing has said ​it “consistently opposed long-arm jurisdiction that ⁠lacks a basis in international law” while India warned Washington that new tariffs could impact bilateral ties. The law allows the president to waive sanctions simply by informing Congress that he has determined that they ​are not in the national interest. “Trump’s latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression,” Beyer said in a statement. Trump had also faced criticism from several US senators, including ⁠some Republicans, ​over a recent diesel deal with Russia in which Trump agreed to lift ​sanctions on Russian exports and Russia agreed to supply diesel to global markets in an effort to lower fuel prices. The lawmakers who criticized the deal said it ​would help fund Russia’s war efforts.

items.originalTitle: Tributes pour in for Lions player Hyron Andrews died in France

items.title: Tributes pour in for Lions player Hyron Andrews died in France
items.summary: Tributes pour in for Lions player Hyron Andrews died in France Vusi.Bafetane Fri, 10/16/2026 - 19:48 view of the Atalante Hotel, where South African rugby player and member of the Lions' team Hyron Andrews died in Sainte-Marie-de-Re, south-western France, on October 16, 2026, on the eve of an Investec Champions Cup match against Stade Rochelais. view of the Atalante Hotel, where South African rugby player and member of the Lions' team Hyron Andrews died in Sainte-Marie-de-Re, south-western France, on October 16, 2026, on the eve of an Investec Champions Cup match against Stade Rochelais. PARIS - South African second-row forward Hyron Andrews of Johannesburg-based side the Lions was found dead at a hotel in France on Friday, on the eve of his team's Champions Cup match against La Rochelle, local authorities told AFP. A source close to the investigation said the 31-year-old lock was found in cardiac arrest in a shower cubicle that was locked from the inside. The public prosecutor in La Rochelle, western France, confirmed that an investigation had been opened to determine the cause of death, which occurred on the island of Ile de Re, and said that an accidental death was currently the leading line of inquiry. An autopsy is due to be carried out, the source close to the investigation said. "This devastating news has sent shockwaves through the international rugby community," the Lions said in a statement. "The former Sharks and Sale Sharks lock forward was a valued member of the Lions family, and his loss will be felt profoundly by his teammates, coaches, supporters and all who had the privilege of knowing him." Andrews had only returned to his native South Africa earlier this year after two years with English Prem side Sale Sharks. He began his career with the Sharks franchise in Durban and represented his country at Under-20 level. "We are heartbroken by the passing of Hyron. He was not only a gifted rugby player, but also a cherished member of our Lions family, having recently joined us this season," added Lions chief executive Rudolf Straeuli. "On behalf of... everyone at the Lions, I extend our deepest sympathies to (his wife) Maighlin, their young sons Hendrix and Emerson and the entire Andrews family. We stand with them in their sorrow and will remember Hyron with great affection and respect." Playing in 'honour of Hyron' The Lions said Saturday's match against La Rochelle would go ahead as planned "in honour of Hyron". It is the first time the Lions have played in the Champions Cup, which brings together the best European and South African clubs. A moment's silence will be held ahead of all Champions Cup and second-tier Challenge Cup matches this weekend in memory of Andrews. "Hyron was a respected member of the rugby community whose contribution to the game and impact on those around him will be remembered with great fondness," said Mark Alexander, president of the South African Rugby Union. "His untimely passing is a devastating loss, and we share in the grief of all who knew and loved him. "The thoughts and prayers of the entire South African rugby family are with Maighlin and all those mourning his loss." Sale director of rugby Alex Sanderson also paid tribute to Andrews, who played 45 times for the club after initially joining as injury cover at the end of the 2023-24 season. "Hyron was just a brilliant guy and a brilliant teammate. He was so skilled on the field but off it, he was always someone you would want to have a beer with," said Sanderson. "He was funny and charismatic in his own unique, dry way and the lads, to a man, loved playing with him and being around him." The tragedy comes exactly 10 years to the day since the sudden death of former Munster coach Anthony Foley, who died in his sleep aged 42 due to a heart rhythm disorder just hours before his team were due to play against Racing 92 in Paris in the same competition. La Rochelle coach Ronan O'Gara was a member of the Racing staff when Foley, a former Ireland international teammate, passed away in October 2016. Bordeaux-Bègles are set to begin their bid for a record-equalling third straight Champions Cup crown later on Friday when they visit Gloucester in the tournament opener. AFP

Wandile Nsibande was arrested last week with two others on public violence and incitement charges stemming from recent anti-immigration protests in Durban. After being granted R1000 bail, Nsibande was intercepted immediately before he could leave the court. Nsibande was previously convicted for kidnapping and robbery in 2009. He was released on parole in April 2022 and was to remain under state supervision until 2034. The department’s spokesperson Singabakho Nxumalo, explaining the processes of a parolee being re-arrested, says the parole board will have to decide on Nsibande’s fate. “Parolees and probationers are subject to specific conditions with which they are required to comply at all times. Failure to adhere to parole conditions constitutes a violation. Where a violation is brought to the attention of the Department of Correctional Services, whether through non-compliance with parole conditions or where an individual is suspected of, or criminally charged with committing an offence, the person must be detained for at least 48 hours. During this period, a parole board must convene to review the individual’s parole placement and determine the appropriate course of action,” explains Nxumalo. Meanwhile, the National Prosecuting Authority (NPA), on Thursday, denied that warrants of arrest were issued against March and March leader Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma and her husband, Xolani Zuma. This came after the advocacy movement issued a statement suggesting warrants for the couple’s arrest had been issued.

items.originalTitle: 'Sportswashing' or investment? Rwanda F1 stirs debate and doubts
items.author: Vusi.Bafetane
items.title: 'Sportswashing' or investment? Rwanda F1 stirs debate and doubts
items.summary: 'Sportswashing' or investment? Rwanda F1 stirs debate and doubts Vusi.Bafetane Fri, 10/16/2026 - 19:21 Rwanda's President Paul Kagame delivers remarks during the announcement of the Formula 1 African Grand Prix at BK Arena in Kigali on October 13, 2026. Rwanda's President Paul Kagame delivers remarks during the announcement of the Formula 1 African Grand Prix at BK Arena in Kigali on October 13, 2026. KIGALI - Viewed by some as "sportswashing" and by others as an overly ambitious, grandiose project, the prospect of a Formula 1 Grand Prix in Rwanda has provoked reaction at home and abroad. The government touts the initiative as a significant "investment in Rwanda's future", slated for sometime in the early 2030s. On Tuesday, Kigali put on a glitzy ceremony to announce the "historic" agreement between Rwanda, the organisation that owns Formula 1, and the International Automobile Federation (FIA). A landlocked country still widely associated with a horrific genocide in 1994, Rwanda has used sports to revamp its image, attract tourists and impress investors with its organisational efficiency. The event promises glamour, replete with champagne-quaffing celebrities, set against the backdrop of Rwanda's verdant hills and rich wildlife, all broadcast to a global audience. Formula 1 markets itself as the third most-watched sporting event on the planet, trailing only the Olympic Games and the FIFA World Cup. However, the project has drawn dismay from some quarters, including Amnesty International, which immediately condemned it as an act of sportswashing. The NGO accuses Kigali of "buying into the world's biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from its appalling human rights record". This same criticism has been levelled against Formula 1 on several previous occasions. In its pursuit of global expansion, the sport has forged numerous partnerships with governments with questionable rights records, including China and Azerbaijan. Sports diplomacy Last year, Rwanda became the first African nation to successfully host the World Cycling Championships. Through its "Visit Rwanda" campaign, Kigali also sponsors several major European football clubs, including Paris Saint-Germain (PSG), as well as the NBA's Los Angeles Clippers. However, while President Paul Kagame is credited with a strategic vision that has driven Rwanda's economic transformation over his decades-long tenure, he has faced repeated accusations from opponents of suppressing political dissent. Reacting to the news, Kenneth Roth, the former director of Human Rights Watch, noted on X Rwanda's "invasion via its M23 proxy of eastern Democratic Republic of Congo". The armed M23 group, backed financially and militarily by Kigali, has forcibly seized vast swathes of the DRC. During the Kigali ceremony, Kagame said it was an "honour" to be selected for Formula 1. He described it as an "investment in Rwanda's future" that would bring "jobs, skills, tourism and new business to our country and our region for decades to come". But one foreign attendee voiced concerns, telling AFP in English: "I am really hoping Rwanda is not chewing what it cannot swallow." Formula 1 is an expensive pursuit and far wealthier nations have already seen their ambitions backfire. The Qatar model India and South Korea, which built circuits specifically to host Formula 1, eventually withdrew as their financial losses mounted. European organisers, including those in France and, more recently, the Netherlands, have encountered similar setbacks. In comparison, Rwanda, despite its economic boom, remains a low-income country with a GDP per capita barely exceeding $1,100. It ranks 159 out of 193 countries on the United Nations' Human Development Index, although it is steadily improving. Critics question whether the hundreds of millions of dollars required to build a modern racetrack might be better spent on healthcare or education, not to mention the tens of millions of dollars F1 Grand Prix organisers typically charge host countries for the privilege of holding the event. A source close to the FIA said Qatar was "supporting" the Rwandan project. The Gulf country is also building a new international airport in Bugesera, 40 kilometres (25 miles) from Kigali, near where the racetrack will be constructed. Jean-Guy Africa, CEO of the Rwanda Development Board, pointed to the "tremendous interest" from the private sector. "You cannot miss out on the 100,000 people who will come. From a business standpoint, you stand to benefit," he told AFP. While several Rwandans told AFP of their pride that their country will soon host the pinnacle of motor sports, Kigali entrepreneur Amon Niyigena, took a more pragmatic view. "The economics of hosting F1 in Rwanda will not be for everyone, but for a tiny percentage of the already rich," he said. AFP

items.originalTitle: Tripartite Alliance partners can still find each other: Analyst
items.author: Richard Brooks
items.title: Tripartite Alliance partners can still find each other: Analyst
items.summary: Despite fears that tensions in the Tripartite Alliance could mark the beginning of the end of the historical pact, political analysts believe the alliance can still be saved. Analyst also believe that ANC, COSATU and SACP pact will be tested at next month’s municipal polls. Tension among the alliance partners surfaced at the COSATU national congress earlier this week. ANC National Chairperson Gwede Mantashe walked out of the congress, protesting against the ANC being billed to speak before the SACP and SANCO. He insisted on speaking at the end, saying it’s in keeping with the alliance’s traditions. But newly elected COSATU President Mike Shingange has warned the ANC and the SACP that the federation will actively lead the alliance, rather than follow passively. The election pact between the ANC, COSATU and the SACP, that has lasted for over three decades, is seemingly on the rocks. Their political dissent stems from the lack of the reconfiguration of the alliance. And this among other things, has prompted the SACP to field its own candidates in next month’s local government elections. But it seems some alliance leaders are frustrated. Even speaking first or last at each other’s gatherings, also became a bone of contention. Earlier this week, the high-level ANC delegation led by party National Chair, Gwede Mantashe, failed to deliver its message of support to the COSATU national congress, after insisting on speaking last. “The message is, you don’t distort the alliance for convenience. You never distort their lives for convenience. You do the right thing, whether it is painful or not. You don’t change it as you like. And one of the things that I will never do is to give up a principle for convenience. I don’t do that as a person.” Newly elected COSATU President, Mike Shingange, promised workers that the trade union federation would lead the alliance, in the absence of a leader. “A way for COSATU actually is become the leader of the alliance. However, in leadership, you don’t declare it is earned and when one of us, as the alliance partners, did not know what will happen tomorrow, and did not know how to bring ourselves together. We will be here. Now we are leading. We will be above you. We will be watching all of you, and we will call you to one house and engage with you. That’s what you decided here.” Political pundits say although the ongoing tension could mark the beginning of the end of the traditional pact, COSATU can play a mediatory role to save the alliance. Politics Lecturer at Wits University, Dr Tshepang Molale says, “We are beginning to see perhaps the beginning of the end of this holy matrimony. However, when you look at the resolution now at the recent COSATU Congress, you’re seeing a more of a reconciliatory posture to say let us not jump the gun. Already, SACP has pronounced that they are going to contest elections, but you see now this new Congress of COSATU. They are saying, okay, maybe let’s let us go back to the drawing board. Let us go back to the negotiation table. So, I am hopefully then this reconciliatory stance, and as a way of trying to call them back, the ANC would have to, or maybe to compromise and then maybe offer some representation to their alliance partners as a way of trying to bring back this matrimony.” However, Molale says these partners can still find each other, as there is not much that sets them apart. Molale adds, “I really don’t think it’s too late. All it takes is compromises and negotiation. And in politics, there are no long-term enemies and there are no long-term friends. And I believe that if, at all, SACP leaders and the ANC, as well, of course, being heralded or facilitated by the COSATU, we might find ways where or areas where they could reach compromises.” With two alliance partners contesting the elections separately, the ANC has since conceded that this could be its worst performance at the polls since 1994. In the 2021 local elections, the ANC received 46% of the vote. And there’s concern that things could get worse, with a record 526 parties standing against the ANC in these elections, and with the SACP not backing it.

items.summary: NBA tells sportsbooks to ban certain bets and parlays: report Siya Tsewu Fri, 10/16/2026 - 18:59 NEW YORK - The NBA told sportsbook partners in a Friday memo to ban certain types of bets and parlays this season that gamblers used in recent wagering scandals, ESPN reported. The prohibition includes a player prop parlay and bets on "under" for players that were part of federal gambling cases that included NBA players Terry Rozier and Jontay Porter, according to the report. The league directed authorized gambling partners, including FanDuel and DraftKings, not to offer bets on such areas as the winner of a game's opening tip-off, players on missing specific shots and under bets for players expected to see under 12 minutes of playing time. "There's a balance between ensuring that we are removing problematic bet types but also ensuring that we don't just move activity into the illegal market," NBA executive vice president Scott Kaufman-Ross told ESPN. "Where we landed right now, we think, is the right balance of those two objectives." Sportsbooks will be banned from offering lines with larger payouts on under wagers. NBA agreements with sportsbook partners permit the league to restrict what wagers they offer. Federal prosecutors said one bettor wagered $80,000 on the under for six statistical categories for Porter in a Toronto Raptors game during the 2023-24 campaign for a $1.1 million payout. Porter admitted removing himself from the game to benefit bettors. Prosecutors claim Rozier was involved in a similar situation while with Charlotte in 2023, although Rozier has pleaded not guilty and denied any wrongdoing. In another memo to clubs, the NBA noted new integrity measures to begin this season, with former NFL star and retired FBI agent Charles Tillman leading training on sport betting rules and enhanced AI looking for unusual betting patterns involving the NBA. The memo said the league seeks to better protect players, coaches and other personnel from threats or harassment from bettors. Article by AFP

The latest deadly school shooting in the United States unfolded on Thursday afternoon when the teenager, who has not been publicly identified, shot through a locked door at the school in central Oregon, according to the Bend Police Department. The teenager killed three children aged 5, 8 and 11 and one teacher before he himself was shot dead by an armed bystander who had pursued him into the school, Police Chief Mike Krantz said at a Thursday evening press conference. Such shootings have become common in the US, with each one reviving debate over gun laws in a country where a right to “keep and bear Arms” is protected under the Constitution’s Second Amendment. BYSTANDER INTERVENED The bystander has not been publicly identified police, though recordings of 911 emergency calls released by authorities include a dispatcher saying he was possibly a father of a child at the school. Oregon Governor Tina Kotek said at the press conference that the bystander “heroically intervened to stop further loss of life.” Beyond those killed, a 7-year-old student and a 54-year-old teacher were taken to hospital with critical injuries. It was not clear if the shooter had any prior connection to the school, which has about 450 students from kindergarten through the fifth grade, roughly ages 5 to 11, and 40 staff members. items.originalTitle: US influence, AI and mistrust cloud Alberta independence vote
items.author: Siya Tsewu
items.title: US influence, AI and mistrust cloud Alberta independence vote
items.summary: US influence, AI and mistrust cloud Alberta independence vote Siya Tsewu Fri, 10/16/2026 - 18:44 TORONTO - The run-up to a referendum in Canada's Alberta region on a future independence vote has been clouded by US political influence and AI-manipulated online content, leaving experts concerned that the results will be contested no matter the outcome. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Thursday that he expected foreign governments, the "United States included", would not get involved in Canadian elections. But the US is already on the scene. President Donald Trump has launched a trade war and repeatedly claimed that Canada should be incorporated into the United States. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called Alberta a "natural partner," while Canada's Globe and Mail newspaper recently detailed contacts between separatist leaders in the province and US Republican operatives. Canada's foreign influence transparency commissioner said in September his office was "aware of concerns" about non-Canadian activities around the Alberta referendum. The minority New Democratic Party (NDP) has advocated for a parliamentary debate on the issue. "None of these things can be taken in a vacuum," NDP Member of Parliament Heather McPherson told AFP. Close Trump allies have also inserted themselves into the online independence conversation. Last week, tech billionaire Elon Musk posted on X after francophone Quebec's separatist party win: "They would be better off. Alberta and Saskatchewan should separate too." Brian McQuinn, the co-director of the Centre for Artificial Intelligence, Data and Conflict at the University of Regina told AFP it "would be folly" to discount the impact this could have in Canada. Along with Americans, McQuinn says he also observed Russian-linked activity pushing the most extreme aspects of the independence debate. This may not directly sway voters but will at least raise the temperature, he said. "If the fire is big and you fan it, it really gets bigger." - AI amplification - AFP | ABED ZAQ Separatist leader Mitch Sylvestre told AFP that US interests "don't play any role" in Alberta "until we win and become government." He insisted his side has a high chance of winning. However, polling firms place support for the future referendum option at about only a quarter of Alberta's population. "A very likely result of this referendum is going to be a community that sees this election as stolen or at least unfair," said Aengus Bridgman, director of the Media Ecosystem Observatory (MEO) at McGill University. Bridgman explained much of the separatist conversation online comes from authentic independence partisans, whose content is often boosted through widespread use of AI. "Their online presence is made bigger through AI use," he said. "It makes it feel better resourced." The MEO also reported on a network of AI-generated videos discussing separatism which garnered over 40 million views and was eventually linked to individuals in the Netherlands. But Bridgman said they appeared to be motivated by profit, not manipulation. Even when AI content did not mislead, its mere presence helps to imply illegitimacy for voters, he said, increasing anxiety. - Widespread distrust - AFP | ABED ZAQ Bridgman said some, not all, separatists are motivated by pandemic-era grievances, with many independence influencers also having ties to the trucker convoy that occupied Ottawa in 2022. "Their evidence of (Ottawa's alleged) authoritarianism is the Covid lockdown," he said. Bridgman and political analyst Lori Williams both noted a general frustration and distrust in Alberta's election agency as well. "Since there's such a large number of potential mail-in ballots and, of course, advance poll ballots involved in this election, people might raise those concerns as well," Williams said She said this apprehension is widespread, beyond separatists, given the complicated referendum vote, which poses nine questions alongside the non-binding separation poll. As Election Day approaches, AFP has already debunked fraud narratives about spoiled ballots and noncitizen voting. Williams anticipates the lasting impact of attempts to influence Alberta's voters seems to be priming many to question the results come October 19. By Gwen Roley Article by AFP

items.originalTitle: Turkey's Salt Lake, life in the shadow of drought
items.author: Siya Tsewu
items.title: Turkey's Salt Lake, life in the shadow of drought
items.summary: Turkey's Salt Lake, life in the shadow of drought Siya Tsewu Fri, 10/16/2026 - 18:23 ISTANBUL - Turkey's second-largest lake has become a stark symbol of a growing water crisis, with drought and intensive groundwater use threatening an ecosystem that supports wildlife, industry and tourism. Known for its stunning natural beauty, Tuz Golu, Turkish for Salt Lake, is a shallow lake that stretches across the heart of central Anatolia about 150 kilometres (100 miles) south of Ankara, the capital. One of the world's most saline lakes, Tuz Golu is an ecologically significant area that is Turkey’s most important breeding site for flamingos and one of the region's key nesting grounds. At sunset, hundreds of flamingos feed in the lake’s waters, their pink and red wings creating striking images against the vast salt flats. AFP | Ozan KOSE This stark and beautiful landscape draws tourists from across Turkey and beyond, who amble through its shallow waters taking photos of their reflections on the mirror-like surface as the light dwindles. But the lake is under threat from a growing water crisis. With a depth of barely 50 centimetres (20 inches), Tuz Golu is located in one of Turkey's most water-stressed regions which has very low annual rainfall. It almost completely dried up in the summer. AFP | Ozan KOSE Five years ago, water shortages that intensified the salinity of the lake meant there was not sufficient water for the young flamingos and around 1,000 died, Turkey's agriculture ministry said. The water crisis is compounded by intensive groundwater use for agriculture in the Konya basin which has increased the lake’s vulnerability to drought. Two years ago, researchers from Ankara's Middle East Technical University found only three percent of precipitation falling across the basin actually reaches the lake. AFP | Ozan KOSE The lake is also Turkey's main source of salt, supplying around two-thirds of its annual production and providing an important source of local employment. Elsewhere along the lake's shores, heavy machinery lumbers across the flats harvesting salt that is taken to facilities to be processed, refined and shipped to buyers at home and abroad. By Ozan Kose Article by AFP

items.title: IEC doesn’t anticipate change of election date over ConCourt ruling
items.summary: The Electoral Commission (IEC) says it does not anticipate a change to the November 4th Local Government Election (LGE) date, despite logistical challenges following the Constitutional Court ruling on the ANC’s candidate lists. The Commission says preparations have been significantly affected by the ruling and its decision to extend the effect of the ruling to 32 other political parties. Addressing the media in Centurion in Pretoria, the commission says the outstanding processes will be completed within a shortened timeframe and under strict supervision. This includes the printing of ballots following the ruling. “At the moment, the commission does not anticipate that these developments will affect the 4 November 2026 election date. However, it is apparent that our logistical preparations have been significantly affected. the logistical operations, therefore, will now have to be conducted within a very truncated period and under very strict supervision,” IEC chairperson Mosotho Moepya explains. items.author: Vusi.Bafetane
items.title: Beyond Game Day | Bongi Mbonambi, VAR Delays And South Africa’s F1 Dream: Who’s Accountable? | 16 October 2026
items.summary: Beyond Game Day | Bongi Mbonambi, VAR Delays And South Africa’s F1 Dream: Who’s Accountable? | 16 October 2026 Vusi.Bafetane Fri, 10/16/2026 - 17:18 South Africa's VAR Delay Reveals Why Sporting Promises Need More Than Political Will The introduction of video assistant refereeing into South African domestic football has become a test of something much bigger than technology. It is testing whether the institutions responsible for the game can translate political commitments into functioning systems, and whether supporters are being given a realistic understanding of what implementation actually requires. Video assistant refereeing, commonly known as VAR, has become an established feature of major international football competitions. Its purpose is to assist referees in reviewing specific match-changing incidents, including goals, penalties, direct red cards and cases of mistaken identity. Yet introducing the technology involves considerably more than purchasing cameras and installing screens. FIFA's Implementation Assistance and Approval Programme requires new competition organisers to complete a structured process involving technology assessments, testing and operational readiness. Its technical standards address matters such as video quality, synchronisation and delays in transmitting footage. Officials also require appropriate training before a system can be used reliably during competitive matches. These requirements expose the gap between an announcement and a working service. A government minister may champion a project and help secure funding, but the system ultimately depends on cooperation between football authorities, competition organisers, technical providers and match officials. The difficulty of turning commitment into delivery South Africa's experience illustrates that challenge. In September 2025, the Department of Sport, Arts and Culture announced an R82 million allocation for VAR implementation and reported progress on procurement, including responses to a request for proposals and alignment with FIFA requirements. By 14 October 2026, however, implementation remained delayed. Following a joint briefing involving Sports Minister Gayton McKenzie and the South African Football Association, SAFA chief executive Lydia Monyepao acknowledged practical challenges affecting the project. The previously targeted start of the 2026–27 domestic season had been missed, with attention shifting towards selected competitions later in the season. The development raises an important distinction. A delayed implementation does not necessarily mean a project has been abandoned, but it does demand clearer explanations of what has been completed, what remains outstanding and who is responsible for each unresolved requirement. In their discussion on Beyond Game Day, Thabiso Sithole and Vata Ngobeni challenged the assumption that VAR could simply be introduced whenever a political deadline was announced. Their exchange drew attention to the administrative and technical processes that must exist before referees can begin using the system. The frustration is understandable. Supporters do not experience football administration through procurement reports or committee meetings. They experience it through decisions on the field, disputed penalties and the confidence they place in match officials. Every public promise creates an expectation that the next controversial decision might be handled differently. Why the rollout matters beyond refereeing Introducing VAR poorly could create a different set of problems. Inconsistent camera coverage, inadequate training or unreliable communications risk undermining the credibility the system is supposed to strengthen. That is why the quality of implementation matters as much as its speed. FIFA recognises both full VAR and the lower-cost VAR Light system, but each operates within defined technical and approval requirements. Choosing an appropriate model is therefore only one part of building a dependable national system. The wider lesson concerns public accountability. Sporting institutions should be judged neither solely by how quickly they announce reform nor simply by whether a deadline slips. They should be judged by the transparency of their planning, the credibility of revised milestones and their ability to demonstrate progress. For South African football, the immediate question is no longer whether VAR is desirable. The harder question is whether the organisations responsible for delivering it can build public confidence before the first review takes place.
